Counterpoint Research latest report points out that the US low-end smartphone market in Q2 2026 is under pricing pressure due to rising memory costs, with smaller manufacturers being hit particularly hard, while larger brands are better positioned to absorb the increase in component costs. Details as follows.

Rising memory costs hit cheap smartphones the hardest

Counterpoint Research data shows that in Q2 2026, the combined smartphone sales of Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google in the US fell 4% year-on-year, while sales of other brands in the market plunged 45%, reflecting how smaller manufacturers struggle to cope with rising component costs.

Counterpoint says that in Q2 2026, sales of smartphones priced below $100 fell nearly 65% year-on-year, which反而 boosted Samsung and Motorola's market share in the prepaid market, because rising component costs have narrowed the price gap between their entry-level handsets and white-label phones.

As for Apple, the report notes that although the company has kept iPhone prices unchanged in the US while raising prices on other products, Counterpoint expects the company to "raise prices for the iPhone 18 series," which is expected to be announced in a few weeks.

Report details:

Analyst Jeff Pu predicted last week that the iPhone 18 Pro would be priced in the range of $1,349 to $1,399, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max at $1,449 to $1,499; multiple reports also indicate that the iPhone Ultra starts at approximately $2,500.

Apple announced its Q3 2026 results last month, with iPhone revenue growing 22% year-on-year to $54.2 billion. The company also warned the market that memory costs and supply constraints would worsen significantly in the September quarter, with particularly notable impact on iPhone, iPad and Mac.
